e.t: This word means “catch,” describing the act of taking hold of or capturing something. It presents catching as an action rather than naming the object being caught. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke 5, at Luke 5:4 and Luke 5:9. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the action of catching.

d: Unable to speak or articulate; speechless.

e.t: This word means “mute”: unable to speak or silent in the ordinary sense. It describes a person whose speech is absent, without stating why or what caused the condition. The word itself names the inability to speak, while the surrounding sentence determines how that inability is being discussed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Mark. These occurrences use the word for a condition involving the absence of speech.

This word describes something that does not fade or lose its lasting quality: “never fading” or “unfading.” It presents what is being described as enduring rather than temporary or subject to decay. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament corpus, in 1 Peter 1:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is something that remains unfaded and enduring.

d: A foreigner, barbarian one who speaks neither Greek nor Latin; as adj: foreign.

e.t: This word refers to a “barbarian,” meaning a person regarded as non-Greek or outside the Greek-speaking world. It identifies someone by language or cultural distinction rather than naming a particular nation or moral quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, and Colossians. Its use can describe the difference between Greek speakers and others, while the surrounding verse determines the precise emphasis. The word itself does not automatically mean savage or wicked.

This word means “gangrene,” a destructive condition in which body tissue decays and the damage may spread. It is a noun naming a serious physical process rather than an action or character trait. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 2:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself presents something harmful that advances and causes increasing damage.

d: So and so, such a one, where the name of the person is known but not used.

e.t: This word means “a certain one,” referring to an unspecified person whose identity is understood from the surrounding context. It functions as a general designation rather than naming the person directly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Matthew 26:18. The precise person intended must therefore be identified from that passage’s context, while the word itself simply points to someone not directly named by the speaker.

This Greek New Testament word means “prisoner” or “prisoners”—a person or group held in custody. It is a noun describing people who are detained rather than free to leave. In this Greek New Testament corpus, it appears twice, both times in Acts 27, referring to prisoners being transported during Paul’s voyage. The plural wording indicates more than one detained person in each occurrence. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific scene, but the word itself identifies those under guard or confinement.

d: (literal: a man who rules by force), a ruler, potentate; also: courtier, member of the court.

e.t: This word means “ruler,” referring to a person who holds authority or power over others. It presents someone as a governing figure rather than merely describing ordinary strength. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Luke, Acts, and 1 Timothy. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a person who exercises authority or occupies a position of rule.

This word means “self-control”: the ability to govern one’s desires, emotions, and actions rather than being ruled by them. It describes disciplined restraint and appears as a quality expected in responsible living. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times across three verses, including a list of virtues and Paul’s teaching about disciplined conduct. Its basic meaning remains focused on inner mastery expressed through outward choices.

d: Each (of more than two), every one.

e.t: This word means “each,” pointing to members of a group one by one rather than only describing the group as a whole. It can identify every individual within a shared situation, responsibility, action, or result. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 82 times, showing that this is a common way to speak about people or things considered individually. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense consistently directs attention to the separate members of a group.

d: (a) to put out or expose a child, (b) to set forth, expound, explain.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to explain” or “to expose,” making something clear by laying it out for others to understand. It can describe a person giving a careful account or openly setting out what has happened or what is being taught. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts, where its basic sense remains an act of explanation or disclosure rather than a hidden or unexplained statement.

This word means “speechless,” describing someone who is unable to speak. It presents silence as a condition affecting a person’s ability to express words aloud, rather than simply choosing not to speak. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 9:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on being without speech. The same meaning is reflected in the English rendering “speechless.”

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “inside,” referring to what is within something rather than outside it. It describes an inward location or position. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, once in Matthew and once in Luke. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a reference to what is within. This is a concise location word, focused on inner position rather than outward appearance or external placement.

me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, iNfinitive

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means to return—to go back after having gone away. It describes the act of coming back to a previous place or point. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Luke. Its central meaning is straightforward: someone or something comes back. The precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself expresses returning rather than remaining away.

gl: what recurs on a day to day basis

e.t: This word means “daily,” describing something that belongs to or recurs each day. It points to a regular day-to-day provision or need rather than something occasional or distant. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice: in Matthew 6:11 and Luke 11:3. Both occurrences are connected with the request for what is needed each day, so the word emphasizes regular, continuing daily dependence. Its precise force in either verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is what recurs on a day-to-day basis.

d: To write, send by letter to.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to write a letter” or “to write to” someone. It describes the act of sending written communication, whether addressing a person or providing written instruction. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament: twice in Acts and once in Hebrews. Its basic sense is practical and direct—communication put into writing rather than spoken communication. The surrounding passage determines who is writing, who receives the message, and what the letter concerns.

This Greek New Testament word means “a sweet smell” or “aroma.” It refers to a pleasing fragrance and can describe something presented or received as having that character. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians, Ephesians, and Philippians. Its basic sense remains focused on pleasant fragrance rather than merely any smell. The surrounding verse determines how that fragrance language is applied in each passage.

d: According to which thing, as, according as.

e.t: This word means “insofar as,” expressing the extent or measure to which something is true, relevant, or applicable. It connects one statement with another by showing the degree in view rather than presenting an entirely separate idea. The word appears four times in the Greek New Testament, across three verses. Its precise force in any particular sentence is determined by the surrounding words, but its central function remains to mark the limit or degree being considered.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to endure” or “to suffer trouble.” It describes continuing through hardship rather than escaping or avoiding it. The word can refer generally to undergoing difficulty and remaining steadfast while doing so. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in two letters: twice in 2 Timothy and once in James. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to cool” or “to cool off.” It describes becoming less hot, whether literally or as a change in temperature. As an action word, it points to the process of cooling rather than simply naming a cool condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 16:24. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its central meaning remains the movement from heat toward coolness.

d: Rough water, a wave, billow, surge.

e.t: This word refers to turbulent water—raging waters or waves. It is used for a powerful, unsettled movement of water rather than a calm surface. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Luke and once in James. Its two approved meanings point to the same central picture: water driven into forceful motion. The surrounding passage determines whether the word describes literal waters or uses wave-like movement as a comparison, but the basic idea remains violent instability and agitation.

d: To become vain or foolish, to be perverted.
me: Verb, Aorist, Passive, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word expresses becoming futile or making something futile—“they made futile,” “to become futile,” or “to make futile.” It describes a loss of useful purpose, effectiveness, or sound judgment rather than simply physical weakness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 1:21. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but the central idea is that something has been rendered empty of its proper value or purpose.

d: To change my place (abode), leave, depart, remove, pass over.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to depart” or “to go on,” describing someone leaving one place and moving onward. It is used for ordinary movement from one location to another, rather than naming a particular kind of journey or destination. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, across Matthew, John, Acts, Luke, and 1 John. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “south,” referring to the direction or region opposite the north. It is a noun used for a geographical direction, a place, or something associated with that region. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, including passages that mention people coming from the south, weather associated with the south, and travel in a southward direction. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: To delay, hesitate, to be slow.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Subjunctive, second, Singular

e.t: This word means “to delay”: to hold back from acting immediately or to postpone an action. It describes waiting rather than proceeding at once. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 9:38, and is rendered “delay.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the postponement of action rather than a description of the action itself.

d: To expose oneself to danger; to be adventuresome, reckless.
me: Verb, Aorist, middle Deponent, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to risk”—to take a chance or expose oneself to possible danger or loss. It describes an act of deliberate daring rather than merely facing difficulty. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 2:30. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the decision to undertake something despite the danger involved.

This Greek New Testament word means “to behead,” describing the act of cutting off a person’s head. It refers to a violent execution or killing by decapitation, rather than to a general defeat or death. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 20:4. Its precise force in that passage is understood from the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the literal act of beheading.

This word means “dove” or “doves,” referring to the familiar bird. It names an actual bird in New Testament passages, whether one dove or more than one. The word occurs ten times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through John. It appears in accounts involving Jesus’ baptism, Jesus’ instruction to his disciples, birds being sold in the temple, and an offering brought to the temple. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

d: (a) prayer (to God), (b) a place for prayer (used by Jews, perhaps where there was no synagogue).

e.t: This word means “prayer” or “prayers”—communication directed to God. It is a noun describing prayer as an act or expression of worship, petition, or seeking God. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 36 times, appearing in contexts that refer both to prayer generally and to specific occasions of prayer. The word is used from Matthew through Revelation, showing that prayer is a recurring part of the New Testament’s description of faithful life and worship.

This word means “colt,” referring to a young animal, especially in the passages where Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem is described. It identifies the animal itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, across 11 verses, and is used in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Its central meaning remains simple: a young animal designated for riding or transport in the passages where it appears. The exact significance of the animal in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “lifeboat,” referring to a small boat carried or used by a larger vessel, especially as a means of escape in danger. It appears three times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts 27:16, 30, and 32. The word identifies a practical vessel connected with a ship’s passengers and crew, rather than describing the larger ship itself. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding account of the voyage.

This word means “security,” referring to a state of being protected or secure. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 3:17. Its basic sense describes secure standing rather than a specific object or action. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise force of the word in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context.

d: To struggle in company with, aid.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to join in a struggle” or “to struggle.” It expresses active participation in difficult effort, emphasizing that someone enters the struggle rather than merely observing it. The wording can describe sharing in a demanding contest or labor with others. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 15:30, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to save”—to rescue, preserve, or bring someone safely out of danger or loss. It can describe saving a person, being saved, or asking whether someone will be saved. The word occurs 106 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through Jude, showing broad use rather than a meaning limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is deliverance or preservation. Matthew 1:21 and Luke 13:23 are among its occurrences.

d: Having three stories; the third story.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word refers to the “third story,” meaning the third level of a building. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 20:9. The word identifies a location or level rather than expressing an action, quality, or person. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning is a building’s third story.

This Greek New Testament word expresses position or agency: something can be “under” another thing, or happen “by” someone or something. Its exact sense depends on the sentence, but its central idea is relation to what is beneath or what exercises an action. It occurs 220 times across the Greek New Testament, so it serves as a common relational word rather than naming an object, person, or event.

This word means “manger,” a feeding place or trough for animals. In the New Testament, it appears four times, all in Luke. Three occurrences are in the account of Jesus’ birth, identifying the place where the child was laid and where the shepherds were directed to find him. Another occurrence uses the same word when referring to an animal being released from its manger. Thus, the word refers to a practical feeding place for livestock.

e.t: This word means “flee” or “to flee”: to move away quickly in order to escape. It is a verb describing the action of getting away rather than remaining in a place or facing a threat. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 29 times, so it can describe different situations while retaining this central idea of urgent departure. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

d: A terrible sight, cause of terror, an object of fear.

e.t: This word refers to a “fearful event” or “fearful thing”—something that causes alarm or dread. It names the frightening occurrence itself rather than describing fear as an emotion felt inwardly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 21:11. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the passage around it. Its central meaning remains something genuinely alarming or terrifying.

This word means a tunic or tunics, referring to a basic garment worn as clothing. It describes an item of dress rather than a person, action, or inner quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, showing repeated reference to this ordinary piece of clothing. The exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself names the garment. Its occurrence in passages from Matthew, Mark, and Luke confirms its use in ordinary clothing language.
